preamble: Loss of retroflexion in the lateral, merging the retroflex lateral [ɭ] with plain [l]. The best-documented case is Sinhala, whose script still distinguishes ළ (ḷa) from ල (la), but where the retroflex lateral is no longer phonemic and ළ is pronounced [l] (ළමයා ḷamayā "child" /ləməjaː/). In Dravidian, Brahui merged Proto-Dravidian *ḷ with *l (Krishnamurti 2003). The earlier claim that Standard Hindi merged a historical /ɭ/ into /l/ is not supported: Hindi l in words such as केला kelā "banana" corresponds to ḷ in Marathi केळे keḷe and Gujarati કેળું keḷũ, but the retroflex lateral there is an innovation of the western and southern Indo-Aryan languages (Masica 1991), not a Hindi loss.

examples.note: Retroflex ḷ and ṇ are no longer distinctive in modern Sinhala; historic speech had the retroflex pronunciation.
*ḷ fell together with *l; Brahui's voiceless lateral later arose from the merged set under unclear conditions.
